h1: Why Does Olive Oil Taste Bitter and Catch the Throat?
excerpt: A young extra virgin olive oil bites the tongue and catches the back of the throat, and a first spoonful can make you cough. That is the oil behaving normally, not a bottle that has turned.
keyTakeaway: Bitterness on the tongue and the peppery catch at the back of the throat are flavour attributes of a young extra virgin olive oil, not signs of spoilage. Both fade as a bottle ages, so an oil that tastes of almost nothing is often an old one. Spoiled oil tastes entirely different: crayons, stale nuts or damp cardboard.

intro: A first spoonful of a young extra virgin oil can sting. The throat tightens, a cough sometimes follows, and the obvious conclusion is that the bottle has gone off.
It has not. Here is what the bite really is, and what a spoiled oil does instead.

sections.heading: No, a bitter olive oil is not off

blocks.text: Bitterness across the tongue and a peppery catch at the back of the throat are two of the three attributes trained tasters record as positive in extra virgin olive oil. A spoonful that makes you cough is doing what a young oil does.

sections.heading: What the bitterness and the pepper are

blocks.text: Olives carry compounds called polyphenols, and two of them do most of the talking. Oleuropein and its relatives give the clean bitterness felt across the tongue. Oleocanthal gives the pungency, felt later and lower down, as a catch at the back of the throat.

items: **Bitter** is a taste, on the tongue, immediate.
**Pungent** is a catch in the throat, a beat behind.
**Green olives** picked early carry more of both than ripe black fruit.

sections.heading: A bland oil is usually an old oil

blocks.text: Both attributes fade with time. The pepper goes first, then the bitterness, and last the fruit, until a bottle pours smooth and tastes of very little. Smoothness is not a sign of quality. An oil with no bite left is usually one that has been open a long while.
Air, light and heat set the pace of that fade. What the pressing itself contributes is set out in [what cold-pressed olive oil really means](/blog/what-cold-pressed-olive-oil-really-means).

sections.heading: How a tasting panel describes an oil

blocks.text: A sensory panel scores an oil on three positive attributes and checks it for defects. The tasters work from blue glasses so that colour cannot influence the score, warm the sample in the hand, and describe what they find in a fixed vocabulary.

sections.heading: How to taste olive oil at home

blocks.text: Tasting from a small glass rather than a teaspoon takes a minute and settles the question. Warmth releases the aroma, covering the glass holds it in, and drawing air across the oil spreads it over the palate so the throat gets its turn.

items: **Pour** a tablespoon into a small glass.
**Warm** it, one palm under, one over the top.
**Sip** a little and hold it on the tongue.
**Swallow** and wait. The pepper arrives last.

sections.heading: Which dishes suit a bitter oil

blocks.text: A strongly bitter, peppery oil is a seasoning, and it wants food with enough weight to meet it. On a delicate or sweet dish the same oil takes over and the cook loses what is being cooked. Warmth softens the bite, so a gentle pan mellows it.

items: **Suits it:** bean and lentil soups, grilled lamb, roasted vegetables, tomatoes on bread, labneh and hummus.
**Fights it:** mayonnaise, delicate steamed fish, milk desserts, plain sponge cakes.
**Softens it:** roasting, gentle frying, or stirring the oil into a warm dish.

sections.heading: What a spoiled oil tastes like instead

blocks.text: A spoiled oil announces itself in the nose, before any of it reaches the tongue. Bitterness has no smell; rancidity does. Where a young oil smells green and tastes sharp, a finished one smells waxy and tastes greasy and flat, with no catch at the throat.

items: **Crayons or putty.** The commonest fault, and the easiest to name.
**Stale nuts.** Old walnuts, or the bottom of a peanut jar.
**Wine gone to vinegar.** Sharp and sour, from fermented fruit.
**Damp cardboard.** A cellar smell, flat behind it.

faqs.a: No. Bitterness across the tongue is one of the attributes tasting panels record as positive in extra virgin olive oil. It usually points to a young oil pressed from olives picked green.

faqs.q: Why does olive oil catch the back of my throat?
faqs.a: The catch comes from oleocanthal, a compound the fruit carries into the oil. It is felt in the throat rather than tasted on the tongue, and a slight cough on a first sip is normal.

faqs.q: Does olive oil get less bitter as it ages?
faqs.a: Yes. Pepper fades first and bitterness follows, which is why an oil tasting of almost nothing is often simply old. Air, light and heat speed the fade, so a badly stored bottle flattens sooner.

faqs.q: Can I cook with a bitter olive oil?
faqs.a: Yes, and heat takes the edge off. Gentle frying and roasting soften the bite, so an oil that seems fierce on bread sits comfortably inside a soup, a tray of vegetables or a braise.

faqs.q: How do I tell bitter apart from rancid?
faqs.a: Smell the oil before tasting it. Bitterness has no smell, so a green, fresh aroma with a sharp finish is fine. Crayon, putty or damp cardboard in the nose means the oil is finished.

faqs.q: Is a mild olive oil a lower grade?
faqs.a: Not on its own. Olive variety and ripeness at harvest both produce genuinely gentle extra virgin oils. Mildness only signals a problem when it comes with a waxy smell or a flat, greasy feel.
